## Four patterns cover most process models {.smaller}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
A continuous variable answers *how much*. A binary answers *whether*.
:::

| Pattern | Meaning | Algebra |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Yes/no decision** | z = 1 if the unit is installed, the stream lined up, the contract signed | z ∈ {0, 1}, priced in the objective |
| **Fixed charge** | cost F paid if and only if the activity happens at all | F z in the objective, plus u ≤ M z |
| **Minimum run rate** | a pump that runs at all must run above L | u ≥ L z |
| **Semicontinuous** | the two above, together | u ∈ {0} ∪ [L, M] |

::: {.flag .c-rust}
**Why the link constraint is not optional.** Without u ≤ M z the solver sets z = 0, pays no fixed charge, and still uses u > 0. The binary must be wired to the continuous variable, or it decorates the model instead of constraining it.
:::

::: {.notes}
**This is the commonest error in student models all term.** Say it now, and say it again at the checklist slide.

Ask the room: what happens if you leave out u ≤ M·z? Wait for an answer, do not supply it. The answer: the solver sets z = 0, pays no fixed charge, and still runs the unit at full rate. The binary becomes decoration.

The line to make stick: a binary that is not wired to a continuous variable constrains nothing.

---

**นี่คือข้อผิดพลาดที่พบบ่อยที่สุดตลอดเทอม** พูดตอนนี้ แล้วพูดซ้ำอีกครั้งที่สไลด์ checklist

ถามห้อง: ถ้าไม่ใส่ u ≤ M·z จะเกิดอะไรขึ้น รอให้มีคนตอบ อย่าเฉลยเอง คำตอบคือ solver ตั้ง z = 0 ไม่จ่ายค่าใช้จ่ายคงที่ แล้วยังเดินเครื่องได้เต็มที่ ไบนารีกลายเป็นของประดับ

ประโยคที่อยากให้ติดหู: ไบนารีที่ไม่ได้ผูกกับตัวแปรต่อเนื่อง ไม่ได้บังคับอะไรเลย
:::


## The semicontinuous set is a disjunction, not an interval {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.spec}
[The set]{.eyebrow}

**u ∈ {0} ∪ [L, M]**

the smallest nonconvex set that appears in process models.
:::

::: {.dots}
- **Not an interval** it is not 0 ≤ u ≤ M, because the band between 0 and L is forbidden.
- **Not convex** u = 0 and u = M are both feasible and their midpoint is not.
- **The binary is what makes it expressible** L z ≤ u ≤ M z with z ∈ {0, 1}.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.spec}
[What relaxing z does]{.eyebrow}

Relax z to the interval [0, 1] and the pair of rows

L z ≤ u ≤ M z

sweeps out the wedge between the two lines u = L z and u = M z.

That wedge is the convex hull of the two pieces — the point z = 0, u = 0 and the segment z = 1, L ≤ u ≤ M.
:::

::: {.note}
The wedge is where every difficulty in this session begins. A fractional z buys a fraction of the fixed charge.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**Draw it on the board before showing the slide.** z horizontal, u vertical. Mark the point (0,0) and the segment at z = 1 between L and M. That is the real set.

Then draw u = L·z and u = M·z, so they see the wedge between them is what the relaxation gives you.

Ask what z = 0.5 means physically. Nothing. But the LP thinks it is fine, and that is the source of every difficulty in the next two hours.

**This wedge is the heart of the session.** Get it here and Lectures 2 and 3 follow on their own.

---

**วาดบนกระดานก่อนขึ้นสไลด์** วาดแกน z แนวนอน แกน u แนวตั้ง จุดที่ (0,0) และเส้นตรงที่ z = 1 ระหว่าง L ถึง M นั่นคือเซตจริง

แล้วลากเส้น u = L·z กับ u = M·z ให้เห็นว่ารูปลิ่มระหว่างสองเส้นคือสิ่งที่ relaxation ให้มา

ถามว่า จุดที่ z = 0.5 แปลว่าอะไรในทางกายภาพ คำตอบคือไม่มีความหมาย แต่ LP มองว่าใช้ได้ และนั่นคือที่มาของปัญหาทั้งหมดในสองชั่วโมงข้างหน้า

**ลิ่มนี้คือหัวใจของทั้งคาบ** ถ้าเข้าใจตรงนี้ Lecture 2 กับ 3 จะตามได้เอง
:::


## Worked example: refinery blending with operating reality {.smaller}

Five component streams blended into two gasoline grades — **the Week 4 instance**. Three operating realities were ignored there.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
| Stream | cost USD/t | avail. t | fixed F<sub>c</sub> USD | min run L<sub>c</sub> t |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Reformate | 760 | 3200 | 12 000 | 800 |
| FCC naphtha | 730 | 4000 | 9 000 | 1000 |
| Alkylate | 805 | 2000 | 15 000 | 500 |
| Butane | 510 | 900 | 4 000 | 200 |
| Straight run | 695 | 2600 | 7 000 | 600 |
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.dots}
- **Lining up a stream costs money** a tank, a pump and a transfer line, whether 1 t or 3000 t moves.
- **A running line has a minimum rate** below it the pump cavitates and the metering is unreliable.
- **The tank farm is limited** at most four streams at once, and butane moves only while the straight-run splitter runs.
:::

::: {.spec}
[The model]{.eyebrow}

max Σ<sub>g</sub> p<sub>g</sub> y<sub>g</sub> − Σ<sub>c</sub> c<sub>c</sub> u<sub>c</sub> − Σ<sub>c</sub> F<sub>c</sub> z<sub>c</sub>

s.t. L<sub>c</sub> z<sub>c</sub> ≤ u<sub>c</sub> ≤ avail<sub>c</sub> z<sub>c</sub>, z<sub>c</sub> ∈ {0, 1}

plus every Week 4 row: grade balances, volume windows, octane, vapour pressure, sulfur.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Back to the Week 4 instance they already solved. Say plainly that last week cheated on three things.

Ask before revealing the right column: what does it actually take to line up one stream in a real refinery? You want tank, pump, transfer line — paid the same whether 1 t or 3000 t moves.

Explain the second reality physically: a pump below its minimum rate cavitates and the metering is unreliable. This is an engineering reason, not an invented constraint.

---

กลับไปที่โจทย์ Week 4 ที่นิสิตแก้ไปแล้ว บอกตรง ๆ ว่าสัปดาห์ที่แล้วเราโกงสามเรื่อง

ถามห้องก่อนเปิดคอลัมน์ขวา: การจะเปิดใช้สตรีมหนึ่งสตรีมในโรงกลั่นจริง ต้องมีอะไรบ้าง คำตอบที่อยากได้คือ ถัง ปั๊ม ท่อ ซึ่งจ่ายเท่ากันไม่ว่าจะส่ง 1 ตันหรือ 3000 ตัน

เรื่องที่สองอธิบายเชิงกายภาพ ปั๊มที่เดินต่ำกว่าอัตราขั้นต่ำจะเกิด cavitation และมิเตอร์วัดไม่แม่น นี่คือเหตุผลทางวิศวกรรม ไม่ใช่ข้อจำกัดที่คิดขึ้นมาลอย ๆ
:::


## What the discrete structure costs {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
| Margin | USD |
|:---|---:|
| A. LP, no discrete decisions | 413 439.75 |
| B. + fixed charges and minimum runs | **342 092.31** |
| cost of the discrete structure | 71 347.44 |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;of which fixed charges paid | 47 000.00 |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;of which minimum run rates | 24 347.44 |
:::

::: {.column width="51%"}
| Stream | L<sub>c</sub> | LP u<sub>c</sub> | MILP u<sub>c</sub> |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Reformate | 800 | 3200.0 | 3200.0 |
| FCC naphtha | 1000 | 4000.0 | 4000.0 |
| Alkylate | 500 | 833.0 | 1533.0 |
| Butane | 200 | 574.5 | 633.9 |
| Straight run | 600 | 473.1 | **600.0** |
:::
::::

::: {.flag .c-rust}
**Read the last column.** Straight run was used at 473.1 t in the LP. A minimum run rate of 600 t forces the plant either to move 600 t of a stream it did not want that much of, or to shut the line down entirely. The optimizer chose to run it and paid the difference — and the minimum run rates cost **half as much again** as all five fixed charges combined.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Spend your time on the last column of the right-hand table** — straight run.

The LP used 473.1 t. The minimum run rate is 600 t. So the plant either moves 600 t of a stream it did not want that much of, or shuts the line down entirely. The optimizer chose to run it and paid the difference.

The number to say out loud: minimum run rates cost 24 347 USD while all five fixed charges together cost 47 000 USD. The constraint that looks smaller costs half as much as the one that looks bigger.

---

**ให้เวลากับคอลัมน์สุดท้ายของตารางขวา** straight run

LP ใช้ 473.1 ตัน แต่อัตราขั้นต่ำคือ 600 ตัน โรงงานจึงมีทางเลือกสองทาง คือส่ง 600 ตันของสตรีมที่ไม่ได้อยากใช้ขนาดนั้น หรือปิดสายทิ้งไปเลย optimizer เลือกเดินเครื่องและยอมจ่ายส่วนต่าง

ตัวเลขที่ต้องพูดออกมาดัง ๆ: อัตราเดินเครื่องขั้นต่ำมีต้นทุน 24 347 USD ขณะที่ค่าใช้จ่ายคงที่ทั้งห้าสตรีมรวมกันเป็น 47 000 USD ข้อจำกัดที่ดูเล็กกว่ากลับมีราคาครึ่งหนึ่งของอีกอันหนึ่ง
:::


## Translation table, part 1: propositions over binaries {.smaller}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Exact and dimensionless — no constant is required
:::

| Statement in words | Logic | Linear constraint |
|:---|:---|:---|
| a implies b | a ⇒ b | z<sub>a</sub> ≤ z<sub>b</sub> |
| a and b are equivalent | a ⇔ b | z<sub>a</sub> = z<sub>b</sub> |
| at least one of a, b | a ∨ b | z<sub>a</sub> + z<sub>b</sub> ≥ 1 |
| not both | ¬(a ∧ b) | z<sub>a</sub> + z<sub>b</sub> ≤ 1 |
| exactly one of a set S | | Σ<sub>j∈S</sub> z<sub>j</sub> = 1 |
| at least k of S | | Σ<sub>j∈S</sub> z<sub>j</sub> ≥ k |
| at most k of S | | Σ<sub>j∈S</sub> z<sub>j</sub> ≤ k |
| a and b together imply c | a ∧ b ⇒ c | z<sub>a</sub> + z<sub>b</sub> − 1 ≤ z<sub>c</sub> |
| a implies b or c | a ⇒ b ∨ c | z<sub>a</sub> ≤ z<sub>b</sub> + z<sub>c</sub> |

::: {.note}
Every propositional statement over finitely many binaries can be written this way. These nine are the ones worth memorizing.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not read row by row. Give them two minutes to read it silently, then ask which rows are unclear.

Emphasise **exact and dimensionless**. None of these nine needs a constant. No M, no units, so there is nothing to set wrongly — unlike the next slide, where M appears.

Say these nine are worth memorising. The rest you can look up.

---

ไม่ต้องอ่านทีละแถว ให้เวลานิสิตอ่านเงียบ ๆ สองนาที แล้วถามว่าแถวไหนไม่ชัด

เน้นคำว่า **exact และ dimensionless** เก้าแถวนี้ไม่ต้องใช้ค่าคงที่ใดเลย ไม่มี M ไม่มีหน่วย จึงไม่มีทางตั้งค่าผิด ต่างจากสไลด์ถัดไปที่ M เริ่มโผล่มา

บอกว่าเก้าแถวนี้คุ้มที่จะจำ ที่เหลือเปิดตารางเอาได้
:::


## Translation table, part 2, and how to check one {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
[Definitional equivalences need three rows each]{.eyebrow}

| Statement | Linear constraints |
|:---|:---|
| c ⇔ a ∧ b | z<sub>c</sub> ≤ z<sub>a</sub>, z<sub>c</sub> ≤ z<sub>b</sub>, z<sub>c</sub> ≥ z<sub>a</sub> + z<sub>b</sub> − 1 |
| c ⇔ a ∨ b | z<sub>c</sub> ≥ z<sub>a</sub>, z<sub>c</sub> ≥ z<sub>b</sub>, z<sub>c</sub> ≤ z<sub>a</sub> + z<sub>b</sub> |

[Where continuous variables enter, and M appears]{.eyebrow}

| Statement | Linear constraint |
|:---|:---|
| if a then u ≤ U<sub>1</sub>, else u ≤ U<sub>2</sub> | u ≤ U<sub>1</sub> z<sub>a</sub> + U<sub>2</sub>(1 − z<sub>a</sub>) |
| if a then g(x) ≤ 0 | g(x) ≤ M(1 − z<sub>a</sub>) |

::: {.note}
Everything above this line is exact. Everything below depends on a numerical constant, which is Lecture 2.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.spec}
[Verify, do not remember]{.eyebrow}

Enumerate all 2<sup>n</sup> assignments, evaluate the proposition, evaluate the inequalities, and confirm they agree on every row. All ten translations in the notebook pass on every assignment.
:::

::: {.flag .c-rust}
**The control case.** Writing a ⇒ b as z<sub>a</sub> + z<sub>b</sub> ≤ 1 fails the same harness: it is the translation of *not both*, and it forbids the assignment (1, 1) that the implication permits.

**A wrong translation is silent.** The model still solves, still reports `optimal`, and answers a different question. That is the Week 6 theme arriving early.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**The point of this slide is the control case in the red box.**

Writing a ⇒ b as z_a + z_b ≤ 1 is wrong: that is *not both*, and it forbids (1,1), which the implication permits. Run the four-row truth table on the board. It takes under a minute and it lands.

The sentence to say: **a wrong translation is silent.** The model still solves, still reports `optimal`, and answers a different question. That is the Week 6 theme arriving early.

---

**ประเด็นสำคัญคือ control case ในกรอบสีแดง**

เขียน a ⇒ b เป็น z_a + z_b ≤ 1 ผิด เพราะนั่นคือ *not both* มันห้ามกรณี (1,1) ที่ implication อนุญาต ให้ลองไล่ truth table บนกระดานสี่แถว ใช้เวลาไม่ถึงหนึ่งนาทีและได้ผลมาก

ประโยคที่ต้องพูด: **การแปลงที่ผิดจะเงียบ** แบบจำลองยังแก้ได้ ยังรายงาน optimal แต่ตอบคนละคำถาม นี่คือธีมของ Week 6 ที่มาถึงก่อนกำหนด
:::


## Activity 1 · logic to linear {.tint .smaller background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
20 min · pairs · paper, then the board
:::

Translate all eight statements into **linear** constraints in binary variables. Use z<sub>A</sub>, z<sub>B</sub>, z<sub>C</sub>, z<sub>D</sub> for the units, z<sub>1</sub>, z<sub>2</sub>, z<sub>3</sub> for the technologies, u<sub>C</sub> for the run rate of unit C, and z<sub>W</sub> for the warehouse lease.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
1. If unit A is built, unit B must also be built.
2. At most two of the four units may be built.
3. Exactly one of the three technologies must be chosen.
4. If unit A is built, unit B must **not** be built.
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
5. Unit C runs at a rate of at least 20 t per day, or it does not run at all.
6. If total production exceeds 100 t, the second warehouse must be leased.
7. Unit D may be built only if **both** A and B are built.
8. At least one of A, B, C must be built, and if all three are built a supervisor must be hired.
:::
::::

::: {.punch}
No products of binaries are permitted. At 12 minutes, eight pairs are called to the board, one statement each.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Walk the room during the first 12 minutes.** What you are looking for is item 7 written as z_D ≤ z_A + z_B.

That is the commonest error, and you want it on the board rather than corrected pair by pair. Seeing where it fails teaches more than being told.

Items 5 and 6 are the only two that need a constant. If a pair finishes early, ask them what M should be in item 6 and how they know.

---

นั่นคือข้อผิดพลาดที่พบบ่อยที่สุด และอาจารย์ต้องการให้มันขึ้นกระดาน ไม่ใช่ไปแก้เป็นรายคู่ เพราะการเห็นว่าผิดตรงไหนบนกระดานสอนได้มากกว่า

## Activity 1 · [ANSWER] · the eight translations {.smaller}

| | Statement | Linear constraints |
|---:|:---|:---|
| 1 | A implies B | z<sub>A</sub> ≤ z<sub>B</sub> |
| 2 | at most two of four | z<sub>A</sub> + z<sub>B</sub> + z<sub>C</sub> + z<sub>D</sub> ≤ 2 |
| 3 | exactly one technology | z<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>2</sub> + z<sub>3</sub> = 1 |
| 4 | A implies not B | z<sub>A</sub> + z<sub>B</sub> ≤ 1 |
| 5 | run at least 20 t/d or not at all | 20 z<sub>C</sub> ≤ u<sub>C</sub> ≤ U<sub>C</sub> z<sub>C</sub>, with U<sub>C</sub> the physical capacity |
| 6 | production over 100 t forces the lease | Σ<sub>j</sub> p<sub>j</sub> ≤ 100 + M z<sub>W</sub>, M = P<sup>max</sup> − 100 |
| 7 | D only if both A and B | z<sub>D</sub> ≤ z<sub>A</sub> **and** z<sub>D</sub> ≤ z<sub>B</sub> |
| 8 | at least one of A, B, C; all three force a supervisor | z<sub>A</sub> + z<sub>B</sub> + z<sub>C</sub> ≥ 1 **and** z<sub>S</sub> ≥ z<sub>A</sub> + z<sub>B</sub> + z<sub>C</sub> − 2 |

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.note}
**The two that generate argument.** 5 and 6 are the only ones needing a constant. 5 is the semicontinuous pattern; 6 is the bridge into Lecture 2. Note 6 is one-way — it does not forbid leasing at low production.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.flag .c-rust}
**The commonest error.** 7 written as z<sub>D</sub> ≤ z<sub>A</sub> + z<sub>B</sub> admits z<sub>D</sub> = 1 with only A built. The pair is correct; the single row 2 z<sub>D</sub> ≤ z<sub>A</sub> + z<sub>B</sub> is also correct but relaxes more weakly.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**Walk the room during the first 12 minutes.** What you are looking for is item 7 written as z_D ≤ z_A + z_B.

That is the commonest error, and you want it on the board rather than corrected pair by pair. Seeing where it fails teaches more than being told.

Items 5 and 6 are the only two that need a constant. If a pair finishes early, ask them what M should be in item 6 and how they know.

## First, what the logic costs on the blend {.smaller}

Two conditions on the tank farm: **Σ<sub>c</sub> z<sub>c</sub> ≤ 4** (cardinality), and **z<sub>Butane</sub> ≤ z<sub>Straight run</sub>** (implication).

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
| Model | margin, USD | streams on |
|:---|---:|:---|
| B. fixed charge + min run | 342 092.31 | all five |
| C1. + cardinality only | 335 539.13 | Ref, FCC, Alk, But |
| C2. + implication only | 342 092.31 | all five |
| C3. + both | **281 361.41** | Ref, FCC, But, SR |
:::

::: {.column width="41%"}
| Cost of | USD |
|:---|---:|
| cardinality alone | 6 553.18 |
| implication alone | 0.00 |
| both together | **60 730.89** |
:::
::::

::: {.flag .c-rust}
**Restrictions interact, and the interaction is not additive.** The implication alone costs nothing, because the unrestricted optimum already runs straight run. Once cardinality removes straight run, the implication also removes butane, and together they cost 60 731 USD — an order of magnitude more than the sum of their individual costs. Total cost of discrete reality: 413 439.75 − 281 361.41 = **132 078.33 USD, 31.9 percent of the LP margin**.
:::

::: {.notes}
**The number to explain is 60 730.89.**

Ask before revealing: cardinality alone costs 6 553, implication alone costs 0. What should both together cost? Most will say about 6 553.

It is 60 731, ten times the sum. The reason: the implication is free while the optimum already runs straight run. Once cardinality removes straight run, the implication removes butane too.

**Restrictions interact, and the interaction is not additive.** Close on 31.9 percent of the LP margin lost to discrete reality.

---

**ตัวเลขที่ต้องอธิบายคือ 60 730.89**

ถามห้องก่อนเฉลย: cardinality อย่างเดียวมีราคา 6 553 implication อย่างเดียวมีราคา 0 แล้วรวมกันควรมีราคาเท่าไร นิสิตส่วนมากจะตอบราว 6 553

คำตอบจริงคือ 60 731 มากกว่าผลรวมสิบเท่า เหตุผลคือ implication ไม่มีราคาเมื่อ optimum เดิมใช้ straight run อยู่แล้ว แต่พอ cardinality ตัด straight run ออก implication ก็ตัด butane ตามไปด้วย

**ข้อจำกัดมีปฏิสัมพันธ์กัน และปฏิสัมพันธ์นั้นไม่ใช่การบวก** จบด้วยตัวเลข 31.9 เปอร์เซ็นต์ของกำไร LP หายไปเพราะความเป็นจริงเชิงจำนวนเต็ม
:::


## The big-M pattern: valid and tight are different words {.smaller}

::: {.spec}
[A constraint that applies only when a binary is 1]{.eyebrow}

g(x) ≤ M (1 − z),&nbsp;&nbsp; z ∈ {0, 1}

**z = 1** — the row reads g(x) ≤ 0 and is enforced.
**z = 0** — the row reads g(x) ≤ M and must be non-binding.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.spec}
[The definition]{.eyebrow}

Any M large enough to make the row non-binding when z = 0 is **valid**, and every valid M gives the same integer optimum. Only the smallest such value is **tight**:

M\* = max { g(x) : x feasible for the other alternatives }

which is itself an optimization problem, usually a small LP.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.flag .c-rust}
**What never to do.** Pick a round number such as 10<sup>6</sup> because it looks big enough.

Two different things then go wrong, and they fail in different ways. The next two slides are one each.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Walk both cases slowly on the board. z = 1: the row reads g(x) ≤ 0 and is enforced. z = 0: the row reads g(x) ≤ M and must not bind.

**Separate valid from tight clearly.** Every valid M gives the same integer optimum — Activity 2 will prove that in front of them. Only the smallest is tight.

Finish on the red box: never pick a round number like 10⁶ because it looks big enough. The next two slides are the two ways it fails, and they fail differently.

---

ไล่สองกรณีบนกระดานช้า ๆ z = 1 แถวอ่านว่า g(x) ≤ 0 บังคับใช้ z = 0 แถวอ่านว่า g(x) ≤ M ต้องไม่ผูกมัด

**แยกคำว่า valid กับ tight ให้ชัด** ทุกค่าที่ valid ให้คำตอบจำนวนเต็มเท่ากันหมด นี่คือสิ่งที่ Activity 2 จะพิสูจน์ให้เห็นกับตา แต่มีเพียงค่าที่เล็กที่สุดที่ tight

ปิดท้ายด้วยกรอบสีแดง อย่าเลือกเลขกลม ๆ อย่าง 10⁶ เพราะดูใหญ่พอ สองสไลด์ถัดไปคือสองวิธีที่มันพัง และมันพังคนละแบบ
:::


## Three recipes for M, in decreasing order of quality {.smaller}

::: {.numbered .n3}
1. **Solve the little LP.** M\* = max g(x) over the rest of the feasible set. Exact, row by row, and what a good modeling layer does automatically.
2. **Use variable bounds.** If g(x) = a<sup>T</sup>x − b with x<sup>L</sup> ≤ x ≤ x<sup>U</sup>, then M = Σ<sub>i</sub> max(a<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub><sup>U</sup>, a<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup>) − b is valid. Cheap, no LP, usually loose by a factor of a few.
3. **Use a physical cap already in the model.** In the blending problem the availability limit caps stream usage, so M<sub>c</sub> = avail<sub>c</sub> is both valid and tight for u<sub>c</sub> ≤ M<sub>c</sub> z<sub>c</sub>.
:::

::: {.flag .c-amber}
**A useful habit.** Write M as a named expression in the units of the row it appears in — `M_c = avail[c]` — never as a bare literal. A big-M with units attached is a big-M somebody can check. In the workbook it gets its own visible cell, `Model!$C$36`.
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide compresses if you are behind, but **do not cut the amber box.**

The habit worth building: write M as a named expression in the units of its own row — `M_c = avail[c]` — never a bare number.

Why: a big-M with units attached is one somebody else can check. A raw number in the middle of a model has no traceable origin. In the workbook it gets its own visible cell, Model!\$C\$36.

---

ถ้าเวลาไม่พอ สไลด์นี้ย่อได้ แต่ **อย่าตัดกรอบสีเหลืองท้ายสไลด์**

นิสัยที่อยากให้ติดตัวคือ เขียน M เป็นนิพจน์ที่มีชื่อและมีหน่วยของแถวที่มันอยู่ เช่น `M_c = avail[c]` ไม่ใช่ตัวเลขดิบ

เหตุผล: big-M ที่มีหน่วยติดอยู่คือ big-M ที่คนอื่นตรวจได้ ส่วนตัวเลขดิบที่โผล่มากลางแบบจำลอง ไม่มีใครรู้ว่ามาจากไหนและถูกหรือเปล่า ในไฟล์ workbook มันมีเซลล์ของตัวเองคือ Model!\$C\$36
:::


## Failure 1: the relaxation collapses {.smaller}

Relaxing z to [0, 1] in u ≤ M z gives **z ≥ u / M**. A large M lets the relaxation buy the stream for a small fraction of its fixed charge.

| Formulation (same 34 rows in every case) | MILP optimum | LP bound | gap, USD | Σ<sub>c</sub> z<sub>c</sub> in LP |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| tight M<sub>c</sub> = avail<sub>c</sub> | 281 361.41 | 379 170.50 | 97 809.08 | 3.6932 |
| loose M = 50 000 | 281 361.41 | 411 575.46 | 130 214.04 | 0.1836 |
| very loose M = 10<sup>7</sup> | 281 361.41 | 413 430.43 | 132 069.01 | **0.0009** |

::: {.flag .c-rust}
**Read the last column.** With M = 10<sup>7</sup> the relaxation switches on all five streams for a total z-mass of 0.0009, so it pays 0.09 percent of the fixed charges and its bound is essentially the pure LP value.

**A loose M does not change the answer. It changes how long the search takes to prove it**, because the bound is what branch and bound must close. You will measure this yourself in Activity 2.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Make them look at the last column, Σz in the LP.**

At tight M, Σz = 3.69: the relaxation pays for nearly four whole streams.
At M = 10⁷, Σz = 0.0009: it switches on all five and pays 0.09 percent.

The sentence: **a loose M does not change the answer, it changes how long you wait for it**, because the bound is what branch and bound has to close.

Flag that Activity 2 after the break is where they measure this themselves.

---

**ให้ดูคอลัมน์สุดท้าย Σz ใน LP**

ที่ M แน่น Σz = 3.69 หมายความว่า relaxation ยอมจ่ายค่าใช้จ่ายคงที่เกือบสี่สตรีมเต็ม ๆ
ที่ M = 10⁷ Σz = 0.0009 หมายความว่ามันเปิดทั้งห้าสตรีมโดยจ่ายแค่ 0.09 เปอร์เซ็นต์

ประโยคที่ต้องพูด: **M ที่หลวมไม่ได้เปลี่ยนคำตอบ มันเปลี่ยนเวลาที่ต้องรอ** เพราะขอบเขตคือสิ่งที่ branch and bound ต้องปิด

บอกล่วงหน้าว่า Activity 2 หลังพักคือการที่นิสิตจะวัดเรื่องนี้ด้วยตัวเอง
:::


## Failure 2: the integrality tolerance becomes a hole {.smaller}

Solvers accept z as integral within an absolute tolerance, typically ε = 10<sup>−6</sup>. A value z = 10<sup>−6</sup> is reported as z = 0, while u ≤ M z still permits **u ≤ M ε**.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
| M | flow allowed, t | charge paid, USD |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 3 200 | 0.0032 | 0.012 |
| 50 000 | 0.05 | 0.012 |
| 10<sup>7</sup> | 10 | 0.012 |
| 10<sup>10</sup> | **10 000** | 0.012 |
:::

::: {.column width="53%"}
::: {.spec}
[Made concrete]{.eyebrow}

Set M = 10<sup>10</sup> and fix every z<sub>c</sub> = 10<sup>−6</sup>, which the solver reports as *off*:

- margin obtained: **413 439.70 USD**
- fixed charges actually paid: **0.047 USD**
- true MILP optimum: **342 092.31 USD**
:::
:::
::::

::: {.flag .c-rust}
**Whose fault.** The plan moves ten thousand tonnes through five lines the solution claims are switched off, and it looks 71 347 USD better than the true optimum. The model is not wrong in exact arithmetic. It is wrong in floating-point arithmetic, which is the only kind a solver has. **M × ε is a modeling decision, not a solver defect.**
:::

::: {.notes}
**This is the slide they will remember longest. Give it the time.**

Explain ε first: solvers accept z as integral within about 10⁻⁶, so z = 10⁻⁶ is reported as off, while u ≤ M·z still permits u ≤ M·ε.

Walk down the table. At M = 10¹⁰ it is 10 000 t. Stop there and ask what this plan is claiming. It moves ten thousand tonnes through five lines it says are shut, and looks 71 347 USD better than the truth.

**Closing line:** the model is correct in exact arithmetic and wrong in floating point, which is the only kind a solver has. M times ε is a modeling decision, not a solver defect.

---

**นี่คือสไลด์ที่นิสิตจะจำได้นานที่สุด ให้เวลามันเต็มที่**

อธิบาย ε ก่อน solver ยอมรับ z เป็นจำนวนเต็มภายในความคลาดเคลื่อนราว 10⁻⁶ ดังนั้น z = 10⁻⁶ ถูกรายงานว่าปิด แต่ u ≤ M·z ยังยอมให้ u ≤ M·ε

ไล่ตารางลงมาทีละแถว ที่ M = 10¹⁰ ได้ 10 000 ตัน ให้หยุดตรงนี้แล้วถามว่า แผนนี้กำลังบอกอะไร คำตอบคือส่งของหมื่นตันผ่านสายห้าสายที่อ้างว่าปิดอยู่ และดูดีกว่าคำตอบจริง 71 347 USD

**ประโยคปิด** แบบจำลองนี้ไม่ผิดในเลขคณิตแม่นตรง แต่ผิดในเลขคณิตทศนิยม ซึ่งเป็นชนิดเดียวที่ solver มี M คูณ ε เป็นการตัดสินใจเชิงแบบจำลอง ไม่ใช่ข้อบกพร่องของ solver
:::

## A disjunction, written two ways {.smaller}

::: {.spec}
[The disjunction]{.eyebrow}

⋁<sub>k</sub> [ Y<sub>k</sub> ; A<sub>k</sub> x ≤ b<sub>k</sub> ] &nbsp;&nbsp;with exactly one Y<sub>k</sub> true.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
[Big-M]{.eyebrow}

::: {.spec}
A<sub>k</sub> x ≤ b<sub>k</sub> + M<sub>k</sub>(1 − z<sub>k</sub>), &nbsp; Σ<sub>k</sub> z<sub>k</sub> = 1
:::

::: {.dots}
- **Compact** one copy of x, one row per original row.
- **Weak** a fractional z relaxes every alternative at once, by a large amount.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
[Convex hull, disaggregated (Balas)]{.eyebrow}

::: {.spec}
x = Σ<sub>k</sub> x<sup>k</sup>, &nbsp; A<sub>k</sub> x<sup>k</sup> ≤ b<sub>k</sub> z<sub>k</sub>

0 ≤ x<sup>k</sup> ≤ x<sup>U</sup> z<sub>k</sub>, &nbsp; Σ<sub>k</sub> z<sub>k</sub> = 1
:::

::: {.dots}
- **One copy of the continuous variables per alternative** which is where the extra columns come from.
- **With z relaxed** the projection onto x is exactly the convex hull of the union of the alternatives.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.punch}
The hull form is the tightest linear relaxation any formulation of that disjunction can have.
:::

::: {.notes}
Write the disjunction on the board in words first: choose one alternative, and once chosen you obey that alternative's constraints.

Compare the two forms directly. Big-M is compact — one copy of x — but weak, because a fractional z relaxes every alternative at once by a large amount.

The hull form gives each alternative its own copy of x, so it costs columns, and in exchange its projection back onto x is exactly the convex hull.

The sentence: the hull is the tightest linear relaxation any formulation of that disjunction can have. Nobody can do better.

---

เขียน disjunction บนกระดานก่อน ในรูปคำพูด: เลือกทางใดทางหนึ่ง และเมื่อเลือกแล้วต้องทำตามข้อจำกัดชุดนั้น

เปรียบเทียบสองรูปแบบตรง ๆ big-M กระชับ ใช้ x ชุดเดียว แต่อ่อน เพราะ z ที่เป็นเศษส่วนผ่อนปรนทุกทางเลือกพร้อมกันเป็นจำนวนมาก

hull ให้แต่ละทางเลือกมีสำเนา x ของตัวเอง จึงมีคอลัมน์เพิ่ม แลกกับการที่ภาพฉายกลับมาบน x เป็น convex hull พอดี

ประโยคที่ต้องพูด: hull คือ relaxation เชิงเส้นที่แน่นที่สุดเท่าที่ formulation ใดของ disjunction นั้นจะเป็นได้ ไม่มีใครทำได้ดีกว่านี้
:::

10 ≤ x<sub>1</sub> ≤ 40, &nbsp; 0.3 x<sub>1</sub> ≤ x<sub>2</sub> ≤ 0.5 x<sub>1</sub>

annualized fixed cost 120 kUSD.

::: {.spec}
[Configuration B, large unit]{.eyebrow}

60 ≤ x<sub>1</sub> ≤ 90, &nbsp; 0.5 x<sub>1</sub> ≤ x<sub>2</sub> ≤ 0.7 x<sub>1</sub>

annualized fixed cost 260 kUSD.
:::

Operating cost 1.8 kUSD per unit feed and 3.2 kUSD per unit product in either configuration; the section must deliver at least 25 units of product.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[Row-wise tightest M, by LP]{.eyebrow}

| A row | M\* | B row | M\* |
|:---|---:|:---|---:|
| x<sub>1</sub> ≥ 10 | 0 | x<sub>1</sub> ≥ 60 | 50 |
| x<sub>1</sub> ≤ 40 | 50 | x<sub>1</sub> ≤ 90 | 0 |
| x<sub>2</sub> ≤ 0.5 x<sub>1</sub> | 18 | x<sub>2</sub> ≤ 0.7 x<sub>1</sub> | 0 |
| x<sub>2</sub> ≥ 0.3 x<sub>1</sub> | 0 | x<sub>2</sub> ≥ 0.5 x<sub>1</sub> | 8 |

::: {.flag .c-amber}
A zero means the row is already implied by the other alternative, so it needs no relaxation at all. **Four of the eight rows are in that class**, which no round-number M would ever discover.

::::

::: {.notes}
The right-hand table is the interesting thing on this slide.

**Ask the room what the four zeros mean.** They mean the row is already implied by the other alternative, so it needs no relaxation at all: M = 0.

Four of the eight rows are in that class, and no round-number M would ever discover it.

This is why recipe 1 on slide 15 is to solve a little LP row by row. It is not fussiness — it finds things the other methods cannot.

## The two relaxation regions {.smaller}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Same disjunction, two formulations, two different relaxations
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.spec}
[What the picture shows]{.eyebrow}

The true feasible set is the **union** of the two boxes-with-slopes, A near the origin and B further out along x<sub>1</sub>.

The **convex hull** is the smallest convex set containing both — area **1100**.

The **tightest big-M** region is strictly larger — area **1137.5**.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.flag .c-rust}
**A point that separates them.** (x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub>) = (22.5, 15.75) lies in the big-M relaxation and **not** in the hull.

It is in neither configuration: x<sub>1</sub> = 22.5 is too large for A only in combination with x<sub>2</sub> = 15.75, which exceeds 0.5 x<sub>1</sub> = 11.25, and it is far below B's floor of 60.
:::

::: {.note}
Draw the two regions on the board before showing the numbers on the next slide. The ordering of the areas is the whole argument.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**Draw both regions on the board before the numbers on the next slide.** The ordering of the areas is the entire argument.

Box A near the origin, box B further right, the hull wrapped around both, then the big-M region slightly larger still.

Point at (22.5, 15.75) and ask which configuration it is in. Neither: x₁ = 22.5 is far below B's floor of 60, and x₂ = 15.75 exceeds 0.5x₁ = 11.25 for A.

**Big-M admits this point. The hull does not.** That is the whole difference.

**วาดสองบริเวณบนกระดานก่อนขึ้นตัวเลขในสไลด์ถัดไป** ลำดับของพื้นที่คือข้อโต้แย้งทั้งหมด

วาดกล่อง A ใกล้จุดกำเนิด กล่อง B ออกไปทางขวา แล้ววาด hull ครอบทั้งสอง จากนั้นวาดบริเวณ big-M ที่ใหญ่กว่าเล็กน้อย

ชี้จุด (22.5, 15.75) แล้วถามว่าจุดนี้อยู่ใน configuration ไหน คำตอบคือไม่อยู่ในทั้งสอง x₁ = 22.5 เล็กเกินไปสำหรับ B และ x₂ = 15.75 เกิน 0.5x₁ ของ A

**big-M ยอมรับจุดนี้ hull ไม่ยอมรับ** นั่นคือความต่างทั้งหมด

| Formulation | rows | cols | LP bound | gap % | relaxation area |

- **The hull region is contained in every big-M region** and the ordering of the areas matches the ordering of the bounds.
- **Tightening M is the cheapest improvement available** going from a round 500 to the row-wise tightest costs nothing in rows and buys 91.7 units of bound.
- **Domination guarantees never worse, not always strictly better** here the hull and the tightest big-M give the same bound in the direction the objective points, even though the hull region is strictly smaller.
:::

::: {.notes}
Work down the table and note that the ordering of the areas matches the ordering of the bounds exactly.

**The number to stress:** going from M = 500 to the row-wise tightest M adds no rows at all and buys 91.7 units of bound. Tightening M is the cheapest improvement available.

**And the caveat, said out loud:** here the hull and the tightest big-M give the same bound, 298.744, even though the hull area is genuinely smaller. Domination guarantees never worse, not always strictly better. Do not let them remember it wrongly.

## Formulation strength as a measurable quantity {.smaller}

::: {.spec}
[Definition]{.eyebrow}

integrality gap = (z<sub>MILP</sub> − z<sub>LP</sub>) / z<sub>MILP</sub> &nbsp;for a minimization,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;(z<sub>LP</sub> − z<sub>MILP</sub>) / z<sub>MILP</sub> &nbsp;for a maximization.
:::

::: {.dots}
- **Two formulations of the same problem have the same integer optimum by definition** as Activity 2 demonstrated. They differ only in their LP relaxation.
- **F1 dominates F2** if the feasible set of its relaxation is contained in that of F2 on every instance. Domination implies a gap that is never worse.
- **The convex hull formulation dominates every big-M formulation** of the same disjunction, because its projection is the smallest convex set containing the alternatives.
:::

::: {.flag .c-rust}
**Why the gap and not the row count.** Branch and bound stops when the incumbent and the best remaining bound meet, so the work is roughly a function of how far apart they start. An extra thousand rows that halve the gap are usually a bargain, and the number of rows is a poor proxy for difficulty.
:::

::: {.notes}
Give the definition cleanly, then stress the three bullets.

The first is what Activity 2 just proved: two formulations of the same problem have the same integer optimum by definition. They differ only in the relaxation.

**The question to ask:** if a thousand extra rows halve the gap, is it worth it? Usually yes, because branch and bound stops when the incumbent and the bound meet, so the work is a function of how far apart they start — not of the row count.

---

นิยาม integrality gap ให้ชัด แล้วเน้นสามบรรทัดในกรอบ

บรรทัดแรกคือสิ่งที่ Activity 2 เพิ่งพิสูจน์ให้เห็น formulation สองแบบมี integer optimum เท่ากันโดยนิยาม ต่างกันแค่ relaxation

**คำถามที่ควรถามห้อง** ถ้าเพิ่มแถวอีกพันแถวแล้ว gap ลดครึ่งหนึ่ง คุ้มไหม คำตอบคือมักคุ้ม เพราะ branch and bound หยุดเมื่อ incumbent กับขอบเขตมาบรรจบกัน งานจึงเป็นฟังก์ชันของระยะห่างตอนเริ่ม ไม่ใช่ของจำนวนแถว
:::

Point at the 20-unit rows as the clearest case: loose M needs a separate capacity row, so it has *more* rows than the tight version and a bound four times worse. More is not worse and fewer is not better.

## Activity 3 · tighten it {.tint .smaller background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
20 min · groups of 3 to 4 · paper
:::

Each constraint is written with a lazy M = 10<sup>6</sup>. For each, derive the **tightest valid M** and give the one-line argument — an upper bound on the left-hand side over the rest of the feasible set.

::: {.numbered .n3}
1. **Zinc-air plant, on/off link for the slot-die coater U3.** x<sub>U3,cath</sub> + x<sub>U3,sep</sub> ≤ M z<sub>U3</sub>. U3 has 3600 h/yr, makes cathode sheet at 0.62 t/h and separator film at 0.48 t/h, and separator demand is 1500 t/yr.
2. **Refinery blend, the second tank-farm bay is leased only above 8000 t.** Σ<sub>c</sub> u<sub>c</sub> ≤ 8000 + M z<sub>lease</sub>. Availabilities total 12 700 t; the grade volume windows are [4000, 7000] and [2500, 5000] t; the octane, vapour pressure and sulfur specifications also apply.
3. **Rented external storage, usable only if the contract is signed.** R<sub>t</sub> ≤ M y<sub>contract</sub>, R<sub>t</sub> ≥ 0. It appears in I<sub>t</sub> ≤ W + R<sub>t</sub> and in the objective at 450 USD per tonne-month, and carries no upper bound anywhere in the model.
:::

::: {.punch}
One of the three has **no finite valid M**. Identify it and say what has to be added to the model.
:::

::: {.notes}
Paper only, no computers. If you are short of time, do (a) and (c) and drop (b).

**Item (c) is the one that matters. Do not cut it.** Walk the room — any group still trying to compute a number for (c) has not understood yet. Ask them where R_t has an upper bound in the model.

Do not tell them which item has no answer. Let them find it.

## Activity 3 · [ANSWER] · the three tightest values {.smaller}

::: {.flag .c-teal}
**(a) M\* = 2 232 t/yr — the lazy M was 448 times too large.** Maximize the left-hand side over the rest of the feasible set. Cathode sheet is the faster product, so all-cathode gives 3600 × 0.62 = 2232 t/yr; separator film is capped at 1500 t/yr by demand and needs 1500/0.48 = 3125 h to make less product, so no mix beats all-cathode.
:::

**(b) M\* = 2 782.5 t — and the two cheaper recipes are both loose.**

| recipe | M, t | source of the bound |
|:---|---:|:---|
| availability sum | 4 700.0 | 12 700 − 8 000, ignores the volume windows |
| grade volume caps | 4 000.0 | 7 000 + 5 000 − 8 000, ignores the quality rows |
| LP over the feasible set | **2 782.5** | max Σ<sub>c</sub> u<sub>c</sub> = 10 782.47, so M\* = 10 782.47 − 8 000 |

The blender cannot reach 12 000 t because the octane floor on Premium and the vapour pressure and sulfur caps limit how much of the cheap high-RVP, high-sulfur streams may enter.

::: {.flag .c-rust}
**(c) No finite valid M exists, and a bigger number is not the fix.** R<sub>t</sub> has no upper bound, so max R<sub>t</sub> is +∞ and no finite M leaves the row non-binding when y = 1. Whatever number you write becomes a silent, undocumented capacity limit on rented storage. The fix is physical: the contract offers at most 500 t per month, so add R<sub>t</sub> ≤ 500, and then M\* = 500 t.
:::

::: {.notes}
(a) M drops from 10⁶ to 2 232 — a factor of 448 — from one line of reasoning.

(b) shows that the easier recipes give looser values. 4 700 comes from the availability sum and ignores the volume windows; 4 000 ignores the quality rows. The true value, 2 782.5, needs an LP.

**(c) is the point of the whole activity.** R_t has no upper bound, so max R_t is infinite and no finite M leaves the row non-binding.

The sentence: **whatever number you write becomes a capacity limit nobody knows is there.** The fix is not a bigger number, it is a physical fact — the contract offers at most 500 t per month, so add R_t ≤ 500 and then M\* = 500.

---

ข้อ (a) M ลดจาก 10⁶ เหลือ 2 232 คือเล็กลง 448 เท่า จากการคิดหนึ่งบรรทัด

ข้อ (b) แสดงให้เห็นว่าสูตรที่ง่ายกว่าให้ค่าที่หลวมกว่า 4 700 มาจากผลรวม availability ซึ่งมองข้าม volume window ส่วน 4 000 มองข้ามข้อกำหนดคุณภาพ ค่าจริงคือ 2 782.5 ซึ่งต้องแก้ LP ถึงจะได้

**ข้อ (c) คือประเด็นของทั้งกิจกรรม** R_t ไม่มีขอบเขตบน max R_t จึงเป็นอนันต์ และไม่มี M จำกัดค่าใดที่ทำให้แถวไม่ผูกมัดได้

## Practice checklist {.tint .smaller background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
When you add a binary to a model
:::

::: {.numbered .n6}
1. **State the disjunction in words first.** If you cannot say what becomes impossible when z = 1, the constraint is not ready to be written.
2. **Wire every binary to a continuous variable**, in both directions if there is a minimum: L z ≤ u ≤ M z.
3. **Give every M a name and a unit**, derived from a bound already in the model.
4. **Verify every logical translation on its truth table**, not from memory.
5. **Solve the LP relaxation and record the gap.** One extra solve, and it is the number that tells you whether the formulation is worth improving.
6. **If the gap is large and the model is slow, disaggregate** before buying a faster computer.
:::

::: {.flag .c-rust}
**Two smells.** A declared parameter that no constraint references — a forgotten constraint. And a binary whose relaxed value is 10<sup>−3</sup> at the LP optimum — a big-M that is too large.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the six quickly, then stop on 2 and 5.

Item 2 is what you said at the start of the session. Say it the second time here, as planned.

Item 5 is the habit worth building: solve the LP relaxation once and record the gap. One extra solve, and it is the number that tells you whether the formulation is worth improving.

**The two smells at the bottom:** a declared parameter no constraint references is a forgotten constraint; a binary sitting at 10⁻³ in the LP optimum is a big-M that is too large. Both are ten-second checks.

## Summary {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
[Takeaways]{.eyebrow}

::: {.dots}
- **A binary models a disjunction** and {0} ∪ [L, M] is the smallest nonconvex set in process models.
- **Every propositional statement is a set of linear inequalities** and the translation is checkable on a truth table.
- **A big-M must be valid and tight** too large costs the bound, and M times epsilon opens a hole in the model.
- **The convex hull form is the tightest relaxation** of a disjunction and dominates every big-M form.
- **Formulation strength is the integrality gap** and it, not the row count, predicts effort.
:::
:::

**If you have five minutes left**, say these three and stop.
One: a binary is only real once it is wired to a continuous variable.
Two: a loose M does not change the answer, it changes how long you wait, and past a point it silently breaks the model.
Three: the gap, not the row count, tells you whether a reformulation is worth it.

## Further reading {.smaller}

::: {.dots}
- **Williams, Model Building in Mathematical Programming, 5th ed.** Ch. 9 on building integer models — fixed charges, logical conditions, semicontinuous variables — and Ch. 10 on formulation strength and why reformulation beats computation.
- **Rao, Engineering Optimization, 4th ed., Ch. 10** for the standard integer-programming vocabulary and worked formulations.
- **Balas (1985)** Disjunctive programming and a hierarchy of relaxations for discrete optimization problems, SIAM J. Alg. Disc. Meth. 6(3) — the source of the disaggregated hull formulation used in Lecture 3.
- **Grossmann and Trespalacios (2013)** Systematic modeling of discrete continuous optimization models through generalized disjunctive programming, AIChE J. 59(9) — GDP as the process systems engineering framing, and the automatic reformulations available in pyomo.gdp.
- **Edgar, Himmelblau and Lasdon, 2nd ed., Ch. 9** for process-scale mixed-integer applications.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not read this aloud. Point at two entries.

Williams Ch. 9 and 10 is the book that matches this session most closely, and it can be read straight after class.

Balas (1985) is the source of the hull form used in Lecture 3, for anyone who wants to know where it came from.

Mention that `pyomo.gdp` performs both the big-M and hull reformulations automatically — see Grossmann and Trespalacios.
